titleText.es: A veces me aterroriza pensar la cantidad de opciones que tienen otras personas.
titleText.en: Sometimes I'm terrified to realize how many options other people have.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish archive and official xkcd source both identify comic #706, and their title texts are preserved exactly. The authored transcript follows the visible Spanish raster: BUM is localized printed sound text, FIJI is a proper name, and the three printed stars are symbols. OCR omitted BUM and the stars, missed accents in DEBERÍA, SÍ, and CONVERSACIÓN, read ¿NO as 2NO, split twelve words at printed line wraps, and produced one spurious V after VEZ.

regions.labelEs: A VECES ME IMPRESIONA LA CANTIDAD DE OPCIONES QUE TENGO.

applications.explanationEn: A veces is the fixed expression meaning that something happens on some occasions.
Me identifies the person feeling the reaction; singular impresiona agrees with the singular cause headed by cantidad.
Que links opciones to tengo and introduces the description that identifies which options are meant.

regions.labelEs: ES DECIR, EN CUALQUIER MOMENTO, EN CUALQUIER CONVERSACIÓN, PODRÍA DARLE UN PUÑETAZO A LA PERSONA CON LA QUE HABLO, Y SE DESPLEGARÍAN UN MONTÓN DE SUCESOS CON LA CAPACIDAD POTENCIAL DE CAMBIARME LA VIDA.

applications.explanationEn: Es decir introduces a restatement that clarifies the preceding idea.
Cualquier appears before the singular noun momento to mean any moment without selecting a particular one.
Cualquier appears before the singular noun conversación to mean any conversation without selecting a particular one.
Podría gives the imagined possibility, and darle stays in its unchanged -ar form with le attached.
Le is attached to the unchanged action verb dar and identifies the recipient of the action.

applications.exampleEs: DARLE UN PUÑETAZO A LA PERSONA
applications.explanationEn: Dar names giving the blow, un puñetazo names the punch, and a introduces the specific person struck.

applications.exampleEs: DARLE UN PUÑETAZO A LA PERSONA
applications.explanationEn: Attached le marks the recipient, while a la persona states explicitly who that recipient is; un puñetazo lies inside the fragment but does not participate in this duplication pattern.
Con is required by the relationship, la agrees with the feminine person already mentioned, and que links that person to the following description.
The -ían ending presents what the plural events would do in this imagined possibility.
The complete informal quantity expression introduces a large number of the following events.
Capacidad names the ability, de links it to the action, and cambiarme is the unchanged action verb with me attached; potencial only describes the capacity.
Potencial follows capacidad as a descriptive adjective that classifies the kind of capacity.
Potencial stays singular to match the singular noun capacidad; its form is the same with masculine and feminine nouns.
Me is attached to the unchanged action verb cambiar and marks the person affected.
Attached me identifies the affected owner, so Spanish uses the definite article la with the closely associated possession vida.

regions.labelEs: SÓLO MIS REGLAS MENTALES ME IMPIDEN GOLPEARTE, O DESNUDARME, O COGER UN AVIÓN A FIJI. SÍ, ESTAS REGLAS OBEDECEN A RAZONES, PERO ¿NO DEBERÍAMOS EXPERIMENTAR ESA LIBERTAD AL MENOS UNA VEZ EN LA VIDA?

excludedUnits.rationale: FIJI is the printed proper name of the Pacific island country rather than a Spanish lexical target.

applications.explanationEn: Mentales follows reglas as a descriptive adjective that classifies what kind of rules they are.
Mentales takes the plural ending -es to match plural reglas; its form is the same with masculine and feminine nouns.
Me identifies the person prevented, impiden agrees with the plural rules, and golpearte supplies the prevented action without an extra word for English ‘from.’
Desnudarme is the second coordinated action prevented by the earlier me impiden; the shared prevented-person and verb do not need to be repeated.
Coger begins the third coordinated action prevented by the earlier me impiden; the shared prevented-person and verb do not need to be repeated.
Te is attached to the unchanged action verb golpear and identifies the informal singular person affected.
The self-marker me is attached to desnudar while that action verb remains in its unchanged dictionary form.
Coger names taking transport and avión names the means of transport; un simply supplies its article.
Obedecen agrees with the plural rules, and a introduces the reasons that explain them rather than a person being obeyed.
Deberíamos makes a softened proposal about what ‘we’ should do, and experimentar stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
The ending -íamos is added to the full dictionary form deber to express what ‘we’ would or should do.
The surrounding opening and closing question marks turn the statement-shaped sequence into a yes-or-no question; no makes the proposed action negative.
Al menos sets a minimum rather than an exact number of occasions.

regions.labelEs: VALE, DEBERÍA HABER VISTO VENIR ESO.

applications.explanationEn: The -ía ending presents what the speaker says they should have done in hindsight.
Debería gives the hindsight judgment, haber builds a completed action, and visto is the completed-action form of ver.
Visto is the completed form of ver, venir presents eso as figuratively approaching, and eso names what should have been anticipated.

regions.labelEs: ¡PERO NO HAS PODIDO! ¡ESO ES LO BONITO!

applications.explanationEn: Has matches informal singular you, and podido supplies the completed ability connected to the present exchange.
Neutral lo turns bonito into an abstract idea: the lovely or nice part of the situation rather than a masculine object.

excludedUnits.rationale: This printed star is an impact or dazed-state symbol rather than a Spanish lexical unit.
This printed star is an impact or dazed-state symbol rather than a Spanish lexical unit.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of a veces, “sometimes”

cards.questionEn: How do you say “sometimes” in Spanish?
cards.noteEn: This common time expression describes something that happens on some occasions but not always. It normally sits before or after the verb without changing form.
In frequency expressions such as a veces and algunas veces, English commonly translates the whole expression as “sometimes.”

cards.answerEn: me; to me (the person who feels the impression)
cards.noteEn: With impresionar, me identifies the person who experiences the reaction. The thing that causes that reaction is expressed separately and controls whether the verb is singular or plural.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something impresses or strikes someone?
cards.answerEn: Use me, te, le, nos, or les for the person who feels the reaction, then a form of impresionar that matches the thing causing it.
cards.noteEn: The short pronoun identifies the person affected: me for me, te for informal singular you, le for one other person, nos for us, and les for more than one other person. The cause controls the verb: Me impresiona el cuadro uses singular impresiona, while Me impresionan los cuadros uses plural impresionan.
Impresiona is the present form used when one singular thing causes a strong reaction or makes an impression.

cards.answerEn: of; or no separate English word, linking an amount to what it measures
cards.noteEn: After a quantity expression, de introduces the substance or thing being measured. English uses “of” in expressions such as a lot of or the amount of, but may leave de untranslated in others, such as un poco de agua, “a little water.”

cards.questionEn: How do you add information about a named person or thing using “who,” “that,” or “which”?
cards.answerEn: Put que after the person or thing, then add a verb and the information about it.
cards.noteEn: Que links the added description to the person or thing before it. It does not change for masculine, feminine, singular, or plural nouns. The added part needs a verb: la casa que vimos means “the house that we saw.”

example.es: La casa que vimos es azul.
example.en: The house that we saw is blue.

cards.answerEn: The joke treats freedom as the unsettling ability to make a wildly unexpected choice at any moment.
cards.noteEn: One speaker argues that ordinary self-imposed rules hide a vast field of possible life-changing actions. The sudden punch demonstrates that freedom while also proving why another person's options can be frightening; the final response celebrates precisely that failure to predict it.
Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.noteEn: Eh can show that the speaker is surprised or did not understand what was just said.

cards.answerEn: part of es decir: that is; in other words
cards.noteEn: Within the fixed linking expression es decir, es does not independently identify what something is; the two words work together as a clarifying connector.

example.es: No puedo ir, es decir, tendrás que conducir.
example.en: I cannot go; in other words, you will have to drive.

cards.questionEn: How do you restate or clarify an idea with ‘that is’ or ‘in other words’?
cards.answerEn: Use es decir before the clarification.
cards.noteEn: Es decir is a fixed connector that reformulates what came before. It commonly appears between commas and does not change for person or time.

example.es: Llegará mañana, es decir, el martes.
example.en: She will arrive tomorrow, that is, Tuesday.

cards.noteEn: Before a specific moment, en can correspond to English “at.”

example.en: He arrived at just the right moment.

cards.questionEn: How do you say “any” before one singular thing?
cards.answerEn: Put cualquier before a singular noun: cualquier libro, cualquier opción.
cards.noteEn: A noun is a naming word such as libro or opción. Before a noun, cualquiera shortens to cualquier. The noun stays singular even when the meaning is any one out of many. The plus sign in the Spanish prompt means “followed by.”

Podría is a form of poder used for a possible or imagined option. Here the unspoken subject is yo, so it means “I could.” The same written form can also go with one other person or thing when context supplies that subject.

cards.promptEs: poder + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone can, could, or may do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of poder for the person and situation, then keep the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Poder changes to forms such as puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, and pueden for present ability or possibility. Podría can present a possible or imagined option. The following action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.

cards.answerEn: to give him, her, it, or them; to give something to a recipient
cards.noteEn: Darle joins dar, the dictionary form meaning “to give,” to le, a small recipient word. Depending on context, le can point to a man, woman, thing, or singular collective. The recipient may also be named later with a, as in darle el libro a Marta.

example.es: Voy a darle la llave a Marta.
example.en: I am going to give Marta the key.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Short object words can attach directly: conocer + te becomes conocerte, and ayudar + me becomes ayudarme.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone punches another person?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of dar, then un puñetazo, then a before the person punched.
cards.noteEn: Dar changes for the person and time, while un puñetazo names the blow. The a introduces the recipient of the blow. A short recipient word such as le can also mark that same person.

example.es: El boxeador dio un puñetazo a su rival.

cards.questionEn: Why can Spanish use le or les with a verb and then still name the receiver with a phrase beginning with a?
cards.answerEn: Use le or les with the verb, then use a phrase beginning with the word a to identify the receiver explicitly.
cards.noteEn: Le is for one receiver and les for more than one. It normally appears before a conjugated verb, but it can attach to an unchanged verb form, as in darle. The later a phrase clarifies who or what the short marker refers to; Spanish often keeps both pieces even though natural English states the receiver only once. In the prompt, the slash means that le and les are alternatives, each plus sign means “followed by,” and the dots mean that other words may appear between the verb and the named receiver.

cards.questionEn: How do you say forms such as “in which,” “with whom,” or “for whom” when referring back to a person or thing?
cards.answerEn: Put the needed preposition before el que, la que, los que, or las que, matching the earlier person or thing.
cards.noteEn: A preposition is a short relationship word such as en (“in”), con (“with”), or para (“for”). Choose el, la, los, or las to match the gender and number of the person or thing being described; que itself does not change. English may use “which” for a thing or “who” or “whom” for a person.

example.es: Esta es la silla en la que me siento.
example.en: This is the chair that I sit in.

cards.answerEn: the feminine article in la que; helps mean which, who, or whom

cards.noteEn: Hablo is the present form of hablar for yo. Spanish can use this simple present for an action happening now where English naturally uses ‘am talking.’

example.en: I am talking with Marta now.

cards.answerEn: marks that events unfold or play out
cards.noteEn: In the pronominal use desplegarse, events develop or play out. Se is part of that verb use; it does not mean a separate person or thing.
Desplegarían is the conditional form for plural things. With se, it describes events that would develop or play out under an imagined condition.

cards.questionEn: How do you form a Spanish “would” verb such as “would forget”?
cards.answerEn: Keep the whole dictionary form and add a conditional ending such as -ía.
cards.noteEn: The same endings attach to verbs ending in -ar, -er, and -ir. The ending changes for the person: -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, or -ían.

cards.questionEn: How do you informally say ‘a lot of’ something?
cards.answerEn: Use un montón de before the noun.
cards.noteEn: Un montón literally means a pile, but un montón de is a common informal quantity expression for a large amount or number. The noun after de may be countable or uncountable.

example.en: We have a lot of questions.

cards.questionEn: How do you name the ability or capacity to do an action?
cards.answerEn: Use capacidad de, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The action verb keeps its unchanged dictionary form, whose base ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. A pronoun may be attached after that ending, as in adaptar + se = adaptarse. Capacidad names the ability and de links it to the action.

example.en: She has the ability to adapt.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.noteEn: After a noun, potencial describes a capacity or effect that may become real but is not guaranteed.

cards.answerEn: to; of (linking capacidad to an action)
cards.noteEn: After capacidad, de introduces the action that someone or something is capable of doing. English usually uses ‘to’ before that action.

example.en: She has the ability to adapt.

cards.answerEn: to change something closely connected to me; for example, to change my life
cards.noteEn: Cambiar is the unchanged dictionary form, and attached me marks the person affected. Spanish can then use the definite article with the affected person's body part or closely associated possession.

example.es: La noticia puede cambiarme la vida.
example.en: The news can change my life.

cards.promptEs: me arreglan el móvil · van a lavarle el coche
cards.questionEn: How can Spanish identify the person affected through a body part, possession, or other closely connected noun without putting a possessive word before it?
cards.answerEn: Mark the affected person with me, te, le, nos, or les, then use el, la, los, or las before the closely connected noun.
cards.noteEn: The short person word goes before a changed verb, as in le repararon, or attaches to an unchanged -ar, -er, or -ir form, as in repararle. The article matches the related noun, whether it names a body part, possession, service, or closely associated aspect. Natural English often expresses that relationship with my, your, his, her, our, or their.

example.es: Van a lavarle el coche a Ana.
example.en: They are going to wash Ana's car.

cards.answerEn: my; literally the (when me already marks the affected owner)
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses the definite article with a body part or close possession when an object pronoun already identifies the affected owner. Me supplies ‘my,’ so la still agrees with the feminine noun.

The comic uses the formerly common accent in sólo. Current standard spelling normally writes solo without an accent when it means “only,” unless an accent is exceptionally needed to prevent genuine ambiguity.
With impedir, me identifies the person who is prevented from doing the following action. Spanish does not add a word corresponding to English ‘from.’

example.en: The noise prevents me from sleeping.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something prevents someone from doing an action?
cards.answerEn: Put a short pronoun for the affected person before a matching form of impedir, then use the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The unchanged dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Spanish places the person before impedir as me, te, le, nos, or les and does not add a separate word for English ‘from’: La lluvia nos impide salir.

example.en: The rain prevents us from going out.

cards.noteEn: Impiden is the present form of impedir for a plural subject. A short word for the affected person normally comes before impiden, and the prevented action follows it.

example.en: The construction works prevent us from passing.

cards.noteEn: Golpear is the unchanged dictionary form ‘to hit,’ and attached te identifies the informal singular person being hit.

example.en: I do not want to hit you.

cards.answerEn: to undress; to take my clothes off
cards.noteEn: Desnudar stays in its unchanged dictionary form and attached me marks that the speaker performs the action on themself.

example.es: Voy a desnudarme antes de ducharme.
example.en: I am going to undress before showering.

cards.questionEn: Where does me, te, se, nos, or os go when a verb used with one of those words stays in its dictionary form?
cards.answerEn: Attach the matching small word to the end: unir + me becomes unirme.
cards.noteEn: A pronominal verb is learned with se, such as unirse or acostarse. When its action verb remains in the unchanged dictionary form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir, replace se with the form that matches the person and write it as part of the same word: acostarme, unirte, or irnos.

example.en: I want to go to bed early.

cards.noteEn: In Spain, coger is ordinary for taking a bus, train, or plane. In parts of the Americas it can be vulgar, so tomar or agarrar may be preferred regionally.

example.es: Cogemos el tren a las ocho.
example.en: We take the train at eight.

cards.questionEn: How do speakers in Spain commonly say they take or catch a bus, train, or plane?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of coger followed by the means of transport.
cards.noteEn: Coger changes for the person and time, and the transport noun follows it. This is ordinary usage in Spain; in parts of the Americas coger can be vulgar, so tomar or agarrar is often safer there.

example.en: We take the bus every morning.

cards.noteEn: At the start of a statement, sí can acknowledge that a point is true before adding a contrast, often with pero. English may use “yes,” “admittedly,” or “granted” for this use.

example.es: Sí, es caro, pero dura muchos años.
example.en: Granted, it is expensive, but it lasts many years.

cards.noteEn: With a reason introduced by a, obedecer can formally mean that something is caused by or explained by that reason, rather than literally obeying a person.

example.es: Los cambios obedecen a nuevas normas.
example.en: The changes are due to new rules.

cards.questionEn: How can formal Spanish say that something is due to or arises from a cause?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of obedecer, then a, then name the cause.
cards.noteEn: Obedecer changes for the thing being explained, while a introduces its cause. This formal use means ‘be due to’ or ‘arise from’; it is different from a person literally obeying an order.

example.es: El retraso obedece a un error técnico.
example.en: The delay is due to a technical error.

cards.answerEn: to; because of (introducing a cause after obedecer)
cards.noteEn: In the formal cause expression obedecer a, this a introduces the reason or cause that explains something.

example.es: El retraso obedece a un error.
example.en: The delay is due to an error.

cards.questionEn: How can Spanish turn an ordinary statement into a yes-or-no question?
cards.answerEn: Use question marks and questioning intonation; Spanish does not need a separate helper like English do or does.
cards.noteEn: The word order can remain the same as in a statement, especially in conversation. The opening and closing question marks show the question in writing.
Deberíamos is the “we” form of deber used for advice or what ought to happen. The -ríamos ending adds the “would/should” viewpoint: deber becomes deberíamos.

cards.promptEs: debería/deberías… + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone should do something?
cards.answerEn: Use an advice form of deber, then keep the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. Use debería for “I,” “he,” “she,” or formal “you,” deberías for one familiar “you,” deberíamos for “we,” and deberían for a plural subject. The following action verb does not change.
Experimentar can mean to experience a feeling, condition, or situation directly; it need not mean conducting a scientific experiment.

example.en: We want to experience something new.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; begins al menos, “at least”
cards.noteEn: Al combines a and el, but the complete fixed expression al menos corresponds to “at least.”

example.en: We need at least one hour.

cards.questionEn: How do you set a minimum and say “at least”?
cards.answerEn: Use al menos before or near the minimum amount or claim.
cards.noteEn: Al menos is a fixed expression. It can set a numerical minimum, as in al menos dos horas, or soften a claim by saying that it is true at the minimum.

example.es: Invita a al menos tres personas.

cards.noteEn: Menos normally means “less” or “fewer.” With al, it forms the common expression al menos, “at least.”

example.en: There are at least two options.

cards.noteEn: Here una gives the number of occasions rather than introducing an unspecified thing.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; Spanish uses la before a general abstract idea such as vida
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses el or la when discussing an idea in general, while English uses the bare noun without “the.” The article still matches the noun: la vida, la paciencia, el tiempo.
Bum is a written sound effect for an impact or explosion. It can represent a sudden blow, a heavy fall, or an explosive noise.

example.en: Thump! The box fell to the floor.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone should have done something?
cards.answerEn: Use debería, or the matching form such as deberías, then haber, then the action's completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: The completed-action form, often called a past participle, commonly ends in -ado for -ar verbs and -ido for -er or -ir verbs: llamar becomes llamado and comer becomes comido. Haber and that final form stay unchanged; debería changes for the person, as in deberías for informal “you.” This pattern often expresses regret or criticism about a past action.

After a verb such as debería, haber remains in its dictionary form and combines with a completed-action form such as llamado or comido. In this construction, haber is a helper rather than the hay construction meaning “there is.”
Visto is the irregular completed-action form of ver, ‘to see.’ After hemos, it helps form ‘we have seen.’

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone sees an event coming or anticipates it?
cards.answerEn: Use the form of ver required by the larger sentence, then venir, then name the event or thing anticipated.
cards.noteEn: Ver may appear in forms such as veo, vi, or he visto according to the person, time, and surrounding construction. Venir stays in its unchanged dictionary form and presents the following thing as approaching figuratively, so the expression means noticing it in advance.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

cards.answerEn: the (neutral article before an adjective, as in lo mejor)
cards.noteEn: Neutral lo turns an adjective into an abstract idea: lo importante means “the important thing,” not a masculine noun.

example.en: The important thing is to begin.

cards.questionEn: How do you refer to “what is important,” “the difficult part,” or another general quality without naming a noun?
cards.answerEn: Put the unchanged word lo before a masculine-singular adjective: lo importante, lo difícil, lo bueno.
cards.noteEn: Here lo does not stand for a masculine object. It turns the quality into a general idea or aspect, such as lo importante, “what is important.” The adjective stays in its masculine singular form because there is no named noun for it to match.
Bonito can come before a noun when the speaker presents a positive, often personal evaluation. Its ending changes to match the noun: bonita, bonitos, or bonitas.
